                                                                        D ENALI: A Dataset Enabling Non-Line-of-Sight
                                                                        Spatial Reasoning with Low-Cost LiDARs

                                                                      Nikhil Behari1 Diego Rivero1 Luke Apostolides1
                                                                      Suman Ghosh2,1 Paul Pu Liang1 Ramesh Raskar1
                                                             1
                                                               Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2 Technische Universität Berlin
                                                                                       nikhilbehari.github.io/denali




arXiv:2604.16201v1 [cs.RO] 17 Apr 2026
                                         Figure 1. Enabling data-driven non-line-of-sight (NLOS) spatial reasoning with low-cost LiDARs. D ENALI is a large-scale dataset of
                                         72,000 full time-resolved histograms captured with low-cost LiDARs in scenes designed to elicit multi-bounce returns from hidden objects.
                                         The dataset spans 60 object shapes, 100 positions, two lighting conditions, and two LiDAR resolutions. Using these diverse captures, we
                                         demonstrate the NLOS perception capabilities of consumer-grade LiDARs through data-driven methods, and identify key scene, modeling,
                                         and simulation-level limitations that can guide future work in data-driven NLOS inference.

known use of full-histogram returns is for non-line-of-sight
(NLOS) imaging, where late-arriving multi-bounce pho-
tons are used to estimate the geometry of hidden scene re-
gions [9, 14, 16, 38]. Several recent methods have aimed
to leverage neural network-based approaches for NLOS re-
construction [10, 30]; in parallel, recent work has explored
learning data-driven representations for NLOS imaging
[8, 18, 19, 36]. Critically, however, these methods primar-
ily focus on reconstructing hidden scenes with laboratory-
grade LiDAR setups. In this work, we uniquely aim to cap-
ture and quantify the broader NLOS perception capabilities
of deployable, low-cost consumer LiDARs.
Imaging with Low-Cost LiDARs. Advances in con-
sumer hardware have enabled time-of-flight (ToF) sensing
in low-cost, consumer devices (e.g. ams TMF8828 [1] and
ST VL53L8CX [33]). Recent works have demonstrated
that these low-cost consumer LiDARs can be used in iso-
lated settings for depth sensing, material classification, and
NLOS vision [7]; similarly, recent works have shown that

prove hidden obstacle avoidance with NLOS vision [40].            ments corresponding to primary single-bounce reflections (shown

Figure 3. Capture setup. Our capture system is designed to record a large-scale dataset of non-line-of-sight, three-bounce light signals
from a mobile flash LiDAR. The setup includes a low-cost single-photon LiDAR co-located with an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera, both
directed toward a flat relay wall. A hidden object is mounted on a motorized gantry positioned outside their direct line of sight to ensure
only indirect three-bounce returns are measured. An additional overhead RealSense tracking camera observes the entire scene, providing
accurate localization of the LiDAR, relay wall, and hidden object during data collection.

tive tape is applied to improve three-bounce photon returns in the measured LiDAR histograms. Each object is printed from a known CAD

Models and Evaluation. We evaluate four models that dif-
fer in how they use spatial and temporal structure in the Li-
DAR histograms. Each architecture introduces a distinct in-
ductive bias (i.e. from structure-agnostic to fully spatiotem-
poral), allowing us to benchmark how modeling choices af-
fect data-driven NLOS inference:
 Benchmarked models
1. Baseline MLP: Each 3 × 3 × 128 capture is flattened and
   passed through a fully connected network; baseline with
   no spatial or temporal inductive bias.
2. 1D CNN (Time-Only): Pixels are stacked as channels;
   1D convolutions operate along time bins, using temporal               Figure 6. Spatial mapping of NLOS localization accuracy. We
   structure without spatial inductive bias.                             plot RMSE (m) over true gantry positions for a single trained
3. 3D CNN (Spatiotemporal): Convolutions operate jointly                 model (1D CNN) broken down by size/lighting. Accuracy gen-
   over time bins and the 3 × 3 spatial grid; captures local             erally improves for larger (8in.) objects nearer to relay wall. How-
   spatiotemporal features before global pooling.                        ever, different lighting induces distinct spatial error patterns, sug-
4. Transformer (Time-Token Encoder): Each time bin is                    gesting poor separation of object, geometry, and lighting.

sion (RMSE / MAE), (b) object classification (Top-1 / Top-5 / Macro-F1), and (c) size prediction (Precision / Recall / Accuracy). Results
are reported overall and by scene factors; CNN-based models perform best but remain dependent on object size, position, and shape.

                                                                                   and location. Larger objects are significantly easier to de-
                                                                                   tect in histograms: Fig. 6 shows that 8-inch objects can be
                                                                                   localized over a wider spatial region than 4-inch objects,
                                                                                   and Fig. 7 shows consistently higher classification accuracy
                                                                                   for 8-inch objects. Object location is equally important: ob-
                                                                                   jects closer to the relay wall enable better NLOS perception
                                                                                   (Tab. 2), but objects placed too close to the wall cannot be
                                                                                   localized due to overlapping first-bounce and three-bounce
                                                                                   returns (Fig. 6). While scene factors (size, location) influ-
                                                                                   ence both conventional and NLOS perception, our results
                                                                                   show that their effects on NLOS perception are distinct, mo-

3 × 3 capture scenes and train a 1D CNN for NLOS object               We introduce D ENALI, the first large-scale dataset of time-
localization. To study key modeling factors affecting sim-            resolved histograms from low-cost LiDARs for non-line-
to-real transfer, we learn three calibration functions for the        of-sight perception. Our aim is to make NLOS perception
simulated histograms: global scaling, pulse-width match-              scalable, data-driven, and ultimately deployable on every-
ing, and noise matching (details in the supplement). We               day LiDAR hardware (e.g., across phones and robotics).
